title: Step tracing and quality numbers
bridge: A step tag is like the data-testid you put on a React element so Playwright can find it. Except the tag rides on the agent's environment, not on the DOM. Every metric, log and model call of that step carries the same five tags, and one session is one step.
intro: A Nova run has nine steps, and each step spends tokens and can let a problem through. This lesson tags every signal with its step and labels failed runs the same way every week. Then it turns run records into one number per gate.

picture.caption: One env per step tags every signal; the weekly review labels failures; the nightly job turns records into gate numbers.

sections.h: A $4.10 run with no step on it
p: Open the operations dashboard from lesson g1-3 and pick one Nova run. The gateway says the run cost $4.10 and used 310,000 tokens. It cannot say which step spent them, because today every call looks the same.

A Nova run has nine steps: ticket, plan, plan_ok, vm, build, pr, byte, approve and learn. A step is one stage of the run, and each stage is its own Agent SDK session. Every metric, log, model call and Temporal record of that session should carry the same tags. The tags are agent, jira, run, step and harness.version.

The tags travel as resource attributes. A resource attribute is a key=value pair that OpenTelemetry attaches to every signal a process sends (lesson p6-1). Claude Code reads them from the OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES variable. We set that variable once per session, and nothing inside the agent has to know.

The harness version is the fifth tag. It is the version field of harness/package.json and it changes on every harness release. With it, evals and live runs can be split by harness version, so a regression points at a release.

callout.text: When a run goes wrong we need two answers: which step spent the tokens, and which step should have caught the problem. Both need every signal tagged the same way.

p: This file lives in the harness workspace, ai-agents/harness/src/telemetry.ts. The harness itself is G3's; this file is the one piece G1 adds to it. It exports the nine steps, the harness version and one function, stepEnv.
The three blank lines of the ticket's sketch are dropped so it fits one block. Nothing else is removed.
sections.because: Because each step is its own session, the harness builds one environment per step, and the tags ride on it.

notes.text: readFileSync from node:fs reads the package file once, when the module loads.
new URL("../package.json", import.meta.url) resolves relative to this file, so src/ and dist/ both find harness/package.json. The cast tells TypeScript the shape.
HARNESS_VERSION is exported so label-run.ts and the workflow use the same value.
STEPS is the list of nine steps in run order. 'as const' makes it a readonly tuple, so TypeScript knows the exact strings.
Step is the union of those nine strings. A typo like "bulid" fails at compile time.
RunTags is what the harness knows about the run: the agent name, the Jira key and the run id.
stepEnv returns a plain Record<string, string>, because environment variables are always strings.
The runtime check matters when the step comes from JSON or a flag, where TypeScript cannot help.
The five tags in one object. "harness.version" needs quotes because of the dot.
The tags become one string: agent=nova,jira=RH-1234,run=r-42,step=build,harness.version=0.4.1. Claude Code attaches it to every metric and event.
The gateway already knows agent, jira and run: they sit inside the run token from G0-13. Only step and version travel as headers.
ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS adds headers to every model call. A newline separates the two headers; the gateway reads x-ai-agents-step.
A wall: no maxTurns, no maxBudgetUsd, no taskBudget. The backstop lives in the harness and acts between turns, never in the middle of work.
options.env replaces the session's whole environment. Spread process.env first, or the gateway URL and run token are gone.
How a step uses it: model and effort from the routing table, env from process.env plus stepEnv(run, "build").
The Temporal workflow sets the same step and version as search attributes, so the Temporal UI filters the same way Grafana does.

sections.ifInstead: If instead a step's session cannot reach the gateway (connection refused to api.anthropic.com), you passed env without ...process.env, so ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is gone.

sections.h: Temporal search attributes and the dogfood check
p: A search attribute is a typed, indexed field on a Temporal workflow (lesson p7-3). You can filter the Temporal UI by it, the way you filter Grafana by a label. The workflow sets two: Step and HarnessVersion.

In the workflow, define the keys once with defineSearchAttributeKey and set them with upsertSearchAttributes each time the step changes. Check the docs for both functions in @temporalio/workflow; the names are typed, so a wrong type fails at compile time.

The gateway already reads the x-ai-agents-step header. Your task is to check that its token and cost series carry a step label, in vmui, before you trust a dashboard. Then run one dogfood ticket end to end and add up cost by step in Grafana. The sum must equal the run's gateway total; if it does not, one step runs without stepEnv.

callout.text: The version comes from harness/package.json. The release workflow bundles the harness into one file, so check that ../package.json still resolves in the VM. If not, inline the version at build time.

p: The second ticket is a small command for the weekly run review. A run label is a JSON file with three facts. It says where a failed run failed, which step should have caught it, and a cause. The cause is one of the five eval cause labels plus model and unknown.

You run it from an ai-agents checkout: npx tsx harness/src/label-run.ts <run-id> --failed-at build --should-have-caught plan --cause missing_context. The first half of the file reads and checks the flags.
sections.because: Because a failure labelled the same way every week can become a check or a skill line, the label has fixed values.

notes.text: The usage line, so the next person sees how to run it without opening the code.
parseArgs is Node's own flag parser from node:util. No library to install.
The S3 client and the put command from AWS SDK v3, the same package the nightly job uses.
STEPS comes from telemetry.ts, so this file and the tags can never disagree about the nine names.
CAUSES: the five eval causes from results.py plus model and unknown. 'as const' keeps the exact strings.
Destructure the parsed flags as a, and the first positional argument as runId.
allowPositionals lets the run id come without a flag name.
Three string flags. parseArgs rejects a flag it does not know, with a clear error.
note defaults to an empty string. One line, no PHI, no secrets, no customer names: the file lands in a bucket many people read.

p: The second half checks each value against its list, builds the label and writes it to the eval results bucket under runs/<run>/label.json. The nightly job counts labels into ai_agents_run_failures_total with failed_at, should_have_caught and cause labels, and the operations dashboard gets a panel for it.
sections.because: Because the JSON keys are the contract the nightly job reads, the file builds them in one place and refuses other values.

notes.text: oneOf is a small validator. readonly string[] accepts the 'as const' tuples STEPS and CAUSES.
The error lists the allowed values, so the message teaches the vocabulary instead of hiding it.
No run id means the usage line is thrown, and the process exits with code 1.
The label object. The keys are snake_case on purpose: they become label names in Prometheus series.
run and failed_at; a["failed-at"] needs brackets because of the hyphen.
cause, note and labelled_at, an ISO timestamp so a month's labels can be counted.
S3Client({}) takes region and credentials from the environment: your AWS profile on a laptop, never a key in code.
One key per run in the eval results bucket from G1-08, next to the eval JSON files.
ContentType application/json lets a browser or the console show the file as JSON.
One line of confirmation, in the same words the review thread uses.

sections.see: r-42: failed at build, should have been caught at plan
sections.ifInstead: If instead you see '--cause must be one of: too_many_tools, ...', the value is not in the list. Pick one of the seven, never a free text.

sections.h: quality.ts part 1: ready and plan adherence
p: The third ticket adds step-quality numbers to the nightly job from lesson g1-2. Each step has one gate and one number, and the number shows which gate is weak before the end result does. A gate is the check a step must pass: the readiness check, plan approval, green CI, Byte, approval.

The job reads run records from Temporal and the run JSON in S3, and Byte's findings from G2's live metrics. It writes per agent and week: delivery_ready_first_try_ratio, delivery_plan_unplanned_files, delivery_plan_items_not_done, delivery_first_pass_green_ratio and delivery_caught_before_pr_ratio.
Lines 1 to 17 of the sketch are below. The blank line 18 is dropped between the two parts; nothing else is removed.
sections.because: Because each step has one gate and one number, we compute the number from run records, and never from a person.

notes.text: A gate's number, not a person's: the rule for every function in this file.
import type brings only types; the build erases it. The shapes live in metrics/src/types.ts.
readyOnFirstTry returns number or null. null means no data, so a chart does not show a fake 0 (the rule from G1-07).
Only runs of the nova agent count: the readiness check is Nova's gate.
The share of tickets with sent_back equal to 0: they passed the readiness check without going back to the requester.
planAdherence takes one run and the files its PR changed. The approved plan lives in run.plan.
A Set of the planned files, for fast lookups.
unplanned_files: changed files the plan did not name. The Set removes duplicates.
items_not_done: plan items without done, so a plan that was approved but not finished shows.

sections.h: quality.ts part 2: green, caught and fast
p: The second half covers three gates: CI on the first push, Byte before the PR, and the approval itself. First-pass green means the required checks on the PR's first pushed commit were all green. Caught before the PR is the share of important problems the self-review fixed before Byte saw them.
Fast approvals are a list, not a score. Plan or PR approvals given under 60 seconds after the request are posted as run links to the weekly review thread. They flag the run, never rank a person.
sections.because: Because a right answer reached the long way still matters, the gates after the build get their own numbers.

notes.text: required holds the names of the required checks from the ruleset (lesson g0-1), so optional jobs do not count.
reduce finds the earliest check run. ISO timestamps compare as strings in time order, as in lesson g1-2.
Keep only runs on that first commit's sha and in the required set; every one must have conclusion success.
caughtBeforePr also returns number or null.
important_fixed comes from the self-review receipt Nova writes into the PR (G4).
left counts Byte findings that are HIGH or MED and new, so a finding Byte repeats is not counted twice.
fixed divided by fixed plus left. When both are 0 there is nothing to measure, so null.
fastApprovals takes the threshold as a parameter, default 60 seconds.
Date.parse both timestamps, subtract, compare with seconds * 1000. The result is run URLs, never names.

p: The label command and the fast-approval list meet in one 30-minute meeting each week. You open five traces: two at random and the three worst. For each failed or rejected run you run label-run with the three flags. A label seen twice in a month gets a ticket. That is how a repeated problem becomes a check, a lint rule or a skill line.
The delivery-impact dashboard from lesson g1-3 gets a 'Quality at every step' row with the five ratios. The operations dashboard gets the failure panel. Both show agents and steps, never a person.

callout.text: Before you label, read the step tags on the trace. The step where cost jumps is often one step after the step that should have caught the problem.

quiz.q: Why does the harness spread process.env before stepEnv(run, step) in options.env?

options.text: Because options.env replaces the whole environment, and the gateway URL and run token would be lost.
options.why: The SDK's env option replaces, it does not merge; without the spread the session has no ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL.

options.text: So the agent can read HARNESS_VERSION from its shell.
options.why: The version travels as a resource attribute and a header; the agent never needs it as a variable.

options.text: Because the SDK refuses an env without PATH.
options.why: The SDK does not check PATH; the real loss is the gateway URL and the run token.

quiz.q: How do agent, jira and run reach the gateway?

options.text: In the x-ai-agents-step header, next to the step.
options.why: That header carries only the step; x-ai-agents-harness carries the version.

options.text: Inside the run token the gateway minted for the run.
options.why: The token from G0-13 already names agent, ticket and run; only step and version ride on headers.

options.text: In the first line of the prompt.
options.why: Tags never go into prompts; the model would see and could change them.

options.text: A score per approver on the delivery dashboard.
options.why: No number is ever per person; that is the rule for every metric in this course.

options.text: A ratio written as delivery_fast_approval_ratio per team.
options.why: It is a list, not a score; a ratio would turn it into a ranking.

options.text: Run links for approvals under 60 seconds, posted to the weekly review thread.
options.why: They flag the run so the review looks at it; they never rank a person.

words.plain: One of the nine stages of a Nova run; each stage is its own Agent SDK session.
A key=value tag OpenTelemetry attaches to every signal a process sends, set with OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES.
A typed, indexed field on a Temporal workflow that the Temporal UI can filter by.
A JSON file that says where a failed run failed, which step should have caught it, and a cause.
The check a step must pass, such as the readiness check, plan approval, green CI or Byte.
All required checks were green on the PR's first pushed commit.

remember: One session is one step: tag it once, label its failures the same way every week, and give every gate one number.
